That actually wouldn't work. If you were going to dig under a tunnel in this manner, you are undercutting the support. What's more, to maintain the reservoir of water, you're going to have to have a clay core surrounded by coarser grained material to hold it in place. As soon as you destroy the integrity of the clay layer water is able to flow through the ground (as water is want to do), and you'll get piping in the soils under the wall. If this piping occurs under the wall then the whole thing will tip over. This is actually what people were worried about happening with the Oroville Dam. The water overflowing the emergency spillway was undercutting the earthen wall that propped the dam up. If the undercutting went deep enough then the water in the reservoir would have a hydrologically conductive route through the earth under the dam. The water flowing through the ground would literally float the wall for a second, and the whole damn thing would collapse. Same thing would happen here. Would totally kill the tunneler, but it would be a massive undertaking to replace the wall in that section.

yeah. This is actually a really good video series.

Most soils is made up of three grain sizes - sand silt and clay. Sand has a lot of pore space that water can move through, silt is small enough that it gets carried away by water and wind, and clay is even smaller, but it's platey so the grains lock together and water can't get through it. When you get a clay layer on top of a body of ground water and you drill a well through it, the pressure of the clay pushes down on it, and you don't have to pump water ouf of the well because it naturally flows (an artesian well).

For the wall though, the silt particles will be removed from the soil as water flows through it, and the sand particles under the wall will resettle, and you get piping through the soils which undermines the stability of the wall.
